technique_name: Process Injection > Injecting through the LD_PRELOAD process
description: LD_PRELOAD is a Linux environment variable that forces the dynamic linker to load specified shared libraries before all others. Attackers can set it to load a malicious .so file, hooking and replacing legitimate library functions to alter program behavior. Effective only against dynamically linked binaries.
potential_defenses: Monitor LD_PRELOAD environment variable for unexpected values
Check /etc/ld.so.preload for unauthorized entries
Use process memory mapping audits (cat /proc/[pid]/maps) to detect injected .so files
detection_opportunities: Unexpected LD_PRELOAD environment variable set on processes
Malicious .so files in /etc/ld.so.preload
Anomalous shared library mappings in /proc/[pid]/maps
code_examples_patterns: Export LD_PRELOAD=/path/to/malicious.so and execute target binary

technique_name: Process Injection > Injecting Data Using the ptrace Process
description: The ptrace system call allows a process to attach to another process, read/write its registers and memory, and inject code. When /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope is set to 0 (classic mode), any process can ptrace another process with the same UID, enabling dynamic code injection via compiled .so payloads.
potential_defenses: Set /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope to 1, 2, or 3 to restrict ptrace access
Monitor for unexpected PTRACE_ATTACH syscalls
detection_opportunities: Unexpected ptrace attach events on critical processes
ptrace_scope set to 0 (classic unrestricted mode)
Anomalous .so library injection into running processes
code_examples_patterns: Use ptrace(PTRACE_ATTACH, pid) to attach and inject code into target process
Use injector <pid> <libpath> to inject compiled .so payload into target

technique_name: File System Isolation Bypass > chroot bypass
description: Attackers can escape chroot file system isolation by exploiting unisolated network sockets, file descriptors opened before chroot, or named pipes that reference paths outside the jail.
potential_defenses: Use namespaces and containers instead of chroot for isolation
Close all file descriptors before entering chroot
Audit network socket bindings within chroot environments
detection_opportunities: Processes accessing paths outside chroot root
Unexpected network connections from chrooted processes
code_examples_patterns: Exploit pre-chroot file descriptors or network sockets to escape chroot jail

technique_name: Non-Executable Bypass > Noexec mounting option bypass
description: Attackers bypass the noexec mount option by using ld.so to load non-executable shared libraries, using source/. commands to execute non-executable scripts, or using mmap to create anonymous RWX memory mappings and copying payload content into them.
potential_defenses: Combine noexec with nosuid and nodev mount options
Monitor for mmap calls with PROT_EXEC flag
Restrict ld.so preload capabilities
detection_opportunities: mmap calls requesting RWX (PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC) memory
Execution of scripts from noexec-mounted filesystems via source command
code_examples_patterns: Use mmap with PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC to map RWX memory bypassing noexec
Use ld.so to load and execute .so files without executable permission bit

technique_name: System Call Restriction Bypass > Bypassing the Seccomp Filter Blocklist
description: Under specific CPU/kernel configurations, 64-bit programs can invoke 32-bit syscalls to bypass seccomp filters that only block 64-bit variants. Additionally, incomplete blocklists (e.g., blocking mprotect but not mmap) allow attackers to use unrestricted syscalls to achieve the same effect.
potential_defenses: Apply seccomp filters for both 32-bit and 64-bit syscall tables
Use allowlist-based seccomp profiles instead of blocklists
Restrict both mprotect and mmap with PROT_EXEC
detection_opportunities: 32-bit syscalls invoked from 64-bit processes
mmap calls with RWX permissions in seccomp-restricted environments
code_examples_patterns: Invoke 32-bit syscalls from 64-bit process to bypass seccomp filter blocklist
Use mmap with RWX flags when mprotect is blocked by seccomp

technique_name: Address Randomization Bypass > ASLR bypass
description: ASLR can be bypassed through weak randomness (insufficient entropy below 20 bits allows brute-force or address spraying) or through information leakage vulnerabilities that expose memory addresses, defeating the randomization entirely.
potential_defenses: Ensure full ASLR entropy (at least 28-29 bits on 64-bit systems)
Patch information disclosure vulnerabilities promptly
Enable hardlink and RELRO protections
detection_opportunities: Repeated exploit attempts suggesting address spraying
Memory information leakage via vulnerable syscalls or application bugs
code_examples_patterns: Perform address spraying or exploit info leak to bypass ASLR randomization

technique_name: CFI Bypass > CFI Bypass
description: Control Flow Integrity (CFI) can be bypassed by exploiting edge cases in the CFI implementation, such as fine-grained vs coarse-grained checking gaps, allowing attackers to redirect execution flow and achieve arbitrary code execution.
potential_defenses: Use fine-grained CFI implementations
Combine CFI with other mitigations (ASLR, DEP, stack canaries)
detection_opportunities: Unexpected indirect branch targets in CFI-protected processes
Control flow violations logged by CFI enforcement mechanisms
code_examples_patterns: Exploit CFI edge cases to redirect control flow and achieve code execution

technique_name: Shadow Call Stack Bypass > Shadow Call Stack Bypass
description: The Shadow Call Stack Guard (RFG) can be bypassed by simultaneously modifying both the function return address on the normal stack and the corresponding entry on the shadow call stack, allowing arbitrary code execution despite RFG protection.
potential_defenses: Keep RFG/Shadow Stack implementations updated with latest patches
Combine shadow stack with CFI and other control-flow protections
detection_opportunities: Shadow stack mismatch exceptions
Simultaneous stack and shadow stack modifications in exploit attempts
code_examples_patterns: Simultaneously modify return address and Shadow Call Stack to bypass RFG

technique_name: Version Downgrade Attack > Version Downgrade Attack
description: Attackers downgrade system tools, command interpreters, or script engines to older, vulnerable versions, then exploit known vulnerabilities in those versions to carry out attacks. Maps to MITRE T1562.010 (Disable or Modify Software Protection).
potential_defenses: Remove outdated and unnecessary tools from the environment
Implement package integrity verification and version pinning
Monitor for unexpected version changes of system binaries
detection_opportunities: Unexpected version downgrade of system interpreters or tools
Hash mismatch of system binaries compared to known-good baselines
code_examples_patterns: Replace system interpreter with vulnerable older version to exploit known CVEs

technique_name: Signature Verification Bypass > Compatibility Bypass
description: Products that check version numbers before signature verification may skip verification for older versions that did not support signing. Attackers modify the version number field to a lower value, causing the verification step to be bypassed entirely.
potential_defenses: Enforce signature verification regardless of version number
Implement monotonic version enforcement to prevent downgrades
detection_opportunities: Version number field modified to an older value
Signature verification skipped for packages with downgraded version fields
code_examples_patterns: Modify version number field to a lower value to skip signature verification

technique_name: Signature Verification Bypass > Forgery of Private Key Signature
description: If a private key is pre-installed or embedded in a product, an attacker can extract it and use it to sign arbitrary malicious files, bypassing all integrity and signature verification mechanisms.
potential_defenses: Never embed private keys in products; use hardware-backed key storage (TPM/HSM)
Implement key attestation to detect key extraction
detection_opportunities: Unexpected signing operations using embedded private keys
Multiple artifacts signed with the same private key in short timeframes
code_examples_patterns: Extract pre-installed private key and sign malicious payloads with it

technique_name: Signature Verification Bypass > Verification Logic Bypass
description: Attackers bypass signature verification by exploiting logic flaws: (1) accessing the installation interface directly without going through the verification interface, or (2) appending malicious data after the verified portion of a package (verified length A, actual length A+B), or (3) exploiting compatibility scenarios where patch packages skip verification.
potential_defenses: Ensure verification and installation use the same data source atomically
Verify the entire package length, not just a prefix
Enforce signature verification for all package types including patches
detection_opportunities: Package size mismatch between verified and installed data
Installation interface accessed without prior verification step
code_examples_patterns: Append malicious data after verified portion of package (verified length A, delivered A+B)

technique_name: Signature Verification Bypass > OTP Write Protection Not Implemented
description: Devices store the hash of a public key certificate in OTP (one-time programmable) memory for boot-time verification. If OTP write protection is not enabled, an attacker can replace the device public key with their own and rewrite the OTP hash to match, then sign and load arbitrary malicious firmware.
potential_defenses: Enable OTP write protection (fuse blowing) immediately after initial provisioning
Implement tamper-evident packaging for OTP programming stage
detection_opportunities: OTP hash value does not match expected public key certificate
Unexpected public key certificate on device compared to manufacturing baseline
code_examples_patterns: Rewrite OTP hash value before write protection is enabled to inject attacker public key

technique_name: Signature Verification Bypass > Missing Software Integrity Verification for Secure Boot
description: Devices without secure boot support often skip both TPM-based certificate validation and runtime software signature verification. This allows unsigned and unverified malicious software to load and execute at runtime without any integrity checks.
potential_defenses: Enforce software signature verification even on boards without secure boot
Implement runtime attestation to verify loaded software integrity
detection_opportunities: Unsigned software loaded on devices that should enforce signature verification
Missing secure boot verification steps in boot log
code_examples_patterns: Exploit missing secure boot verification to load unsigned malicious firmware

technique_name: Using Files to Bypass > HTML Smuggling
description: Attackers hide malicious payloads within seemingly benign HTML files using JavaScript Blobs and the HTML5 download attribute to smuggle data past content filters and security controls. Maps to MITRE T1027.006.
potential_defenses: Deploy advanced web gateways that decode and inspect HTML/JavaScript content
Enable script block logging and AMSI for client-side detection
Block or sandbox HTML files with embedded JavaScript Blobs
detection_opportunities: HTML files containing JavaScript Blob creation with binary data
Unexpected HTML5 download attribute usage triggering file downloads
Obfuscated JavaScript within HTML payload delivery mechanisms
code_examples_patterns: Embed payload in HTML using JavaScript Blobs and HTML5 download attribute

technique_name: Log Cleanup > Deleting Container and Host Machine Logs
description: After obtaining write permissions for system and service logs within containers and on the host, attackers delete or modify log entries to erase evidence of their activities and evade detection.
potential_defenses: Restrict write permissions on log files
Implement real-time log forwarding to a remote SIEM
Use immutable log storage (append-only)
detection_opportunities: Sudden gaps in log timelines
Log file deletion or truncation events
wevtutil cl (clear log) command execution
code_examples_patterns: Delete EventLog entries: wevtutil cl Security
Remove container log files: rm -rf /var/log/containers/*

technique_name: Log Cleanup > Kubernetes Audit Log Cleanup
description: Attackers conceal K8s cluster operations by clearing local audit log files and severing log upload channels (uninstalling collection agents or blocking network paths to log services), making their activities invisible to security monitoring.
potential_defenses: Generate alerts when log collection fails or agents go offline
Forward Kubernetes audit logs to external immutable storage in real time
Restrict agent uninstallation permissions
detection_opportunities: Kubernetes audit log collection agent goes offline unexpectedly
Network connectivity to log collection endpoints is blocked
Audit log files cleared or truncated on API Server nodes
code_examples_patterns: Clear Kubernetes audit logs and disconnect log collection agents
Block network path to log collection service to prevent log upload

technique_name: Log Service Attack > Creating Extra Long Annotations to Parse Logs Fails
description: Attackers create Kubernetes resources with excessively long annotation fields that trigger log parsing truncation in collection agents. The truncated logs cause sensitive attack data to be cut off, allowing malicious operations to bypass audit rules and evade intrusion detection.
potential_defenses: Implement proper field length handling in log parsers without silent truncation
Alert on annotation fields exceeding expected length thresholds
Validate log completeness at ingestion time
detection_opportunities: Kubernetes annotations with abnormally long field values
Log parsing errors or truncation warnings in collection agents
Audit log entries with missing or truncated fields
code_examples_patterns: Create extra-long annotations to trigger log truncation and bypass audit rules

technique_name: Concealment During Access > Accessing the K8s API Server via Proxy or Anonymous Network
description: Attackers route Kubernetes API Server requests through proxies or anonymous networks (e.g., Tor) to obscure their true source IP address, making attack attribution and source tracing significantly more difficult.
potential_defenses: Enforce mTLS authentication for all API Server connections
Implement network-level access controls and IP allowlisting
Deploy API Server audit logging with connection metadata
detection_opportunities: API Server requests originating from known proxy or Tor exit node IPs
Anonymous or unauthenticated API Server access attempts
code_examples_patterns: Route K8s API requests through proxy or anonymous network to hide attack source

technique_name: Concealment During Operation > Using System Pods to Masquerade
description: Attackers create pods with names similar to legitimate K8s built-in system pods, or embed backdoor code within common system pods, achieving covert and persistent access that blends in with normal cluster operations.
potential_defenses: Restrict kubectl execution permissions and separate from application users
Implement pod admission controllers with name validation
Maintain an inventory of expected system pods and alert on deviations
detection_opportunities: Pods with names similar to but not matching known system pods
Unexpected pods in system namespaces (kube-system, kube-public)
Pod image hash mismatch for supposed system pods
code_examples_patterns: Create pods with names similar to built-in K8s system pods for concealment

technique_name: Concealment During Operation > Creating a Shadow API Server
description: Attackers replicate the native K8s API Server configuration with modified parameters (disabled authentication, anonymous access, HTTP instead of HTTPS) to create a shadow API Server. This provides direct anonymous access to etcd data while making subsequent activities invisible in official audit logs.
potential_defenses: Restrict kubectl and API Server binary execution permissions
Monitor for unauthorized API Server process instances
Implement network policies to prevent rogue API Server endpoints
detection_opportunities: Multiple API Server processes running on the cluster
API Server instances with authentication disabled or using HTTP
Pods providing API-like services outside the control plane namespace
code_examples_patterns: Replicate API Server config with auth disabled to create anonymous shadow API

technique_name: Concealment During Operation > Hidden Files and Processes
description: Attackers conceal malicious activities by hiding processes and files involved in illegal operations, using techniques such as hidden file naming conventions, process name spoofing, and in-memory execution to avoid detection.
potential_defenses: Apply latest security patches and harden device security configurations
Use file integrity monitoring (FIM) to detect hidden file creation
Monitor for process name spoofing and in-memory execution
detection_opportunities: Files with hidden naming conventions (dotfiles, Unicode tricks)
Processes with names mimicking legitimate system processes
In-memory execution without corresponding disk artifacts
code_examples_patterns: Use hidden file prefixes and process name spoofing to conceal malicious artifacts

technique_name: Remove Antivirus Software Components > Clean Up Security Product Agent
description: After gaining cluster management permissions or escaping to the host, attackers remove security product probes and agents, compromising log integrity and making subsequent attack behaviors invisible to auditing and detection tools.
potential_defenses: Run security agents as daemon processes under high-privilege system accounts
Generate immediate alerts when security agents go offline
Implement agent health monitoring with redundant heartbeat mechanisms
detection_opportunities: Security agent process terminated unexpectedly
Agent heartbeat/telemetry stops arriving at management console
Security product binaries or configuration files deleted from disk
code_examples_patterns: Kill security agent daemon processes and remove their file system artifacts
